translationRepairs: An ancestor named Cheng had served as Administrator of Dunqiu under the dynasty's High Ancestor, and the family made its home there.
His great-great-grandfather Cheng had served as Administrator of Dunqiu, and the family made its home there.
In this genealogical introduction, 高祖 is Dou Jin's great-great-grandfather and 成 is that ancestor's name; the current English wrongly turns 高祖 into a ruler under whom Cheng served.
He rose from Doctor of the Secretariat to Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Secretariat, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fanyang, and was given the additional rank of General for Pacifying the Distance.
He rose from Doctor of the Secretariat to Attendant Gentleman of the Secretariat, was enfeoffed as Viscount of Fanyang, and was given the additional rank of General for Pacifying the Distance.
中書侍郎 is Attendant Gentleman of the Secretariat, while the noble rank 子 in 繁陽子 is viscount; both offices are mistranslated in the current sentence.

Early in the Xingguang era, Jin's son-in-law Moduo, a staff officer attached to the Prince of Yulin, was chosen to marry Princess Linjing. Jin urged Moduo to refuse the match on one pretext or another, and words of slander and imprecation were involved; Jin was executed along with Moduo.

Early in the Xingguang era, Jin's son-in-law Sima Moduo, Duke of Yulin, was chosen to marry Princess Linjing. Jin urged Moduo to refuse the match on one pretext or another, and words of slander and imprecation were involved; Jin was executed along with Moduo.
鬱林公 is Sima Moduo's ducal title and 司馬 is his surname. The current parsing as an unnamed Moduo serving a Prince of Yulin is unsupported.
Yan was sincere, thick, and cautious; in conversation with others he never touched on inner-court affairs.
Yan was honest and generous, cautious and discreet; in conversation with others he never touched on inner-court affairs.
The repair correctly removes the calque 'thick,' but 'substantial' remains stiff for 質厚. 'Honest and generous' pairs naturally with 慎密, 'cautious and discreet.'
His son Zongzhi entered service as Palace Scribe and headed the Inner Secretariat.
His son Zongzhi entered service as Cavalier Attendant and headed the Inner Secretariat.
中散 denotes the court office Cavalier Attendant, not a scribal post. The correction is necessary, but the redundant romanized parenthesis makes the proposed English less polished.
His son Zongzhi, on first entering service, became Palace Scribe and headed the Inner Secretariat.
His son Zongzhi, on first entering service, became Cavalier Attendant and headed the Inner Secretariat.
The literal field also mistakes 中散 for a scribe. 'Cavalier Attendant' supplies the office cleanly without the proposal's unnecessary romanized parenthesis.
When Emperor Shizu crossed the Yangzi, he was granted the title Marquis of Gaoxiang.
When Emperor Shizu reached the Yangzi, Zongzhi was granted the title Marquis of Gaoxiang.
臨江 says that Shizu reached or came to the river, not that he crossed it. Naming Zongzhi also removes the proposal's ambiguous pronoun and agrees with the surrounding biography.
Sun Yan, whose courtesy name was Changlin, was capable and effective in office.
His grandson Yan, whose courtesy name was Changlin, was capable and effective in office.
Within this genealogy 孫 marks Yan as a grandson; it is not the surname Sun. The replacement restores the kinship transition and Yan's actual name.
Sun Yan, courtesy name Changlin, was capable and effective.
His grandson Yan, courtesy name Changlin, was capable and effective.
The literal field makes the same segmentation error: 孫 is the kinship term 'grandson,' followed by the personal name 琰.
Du Chao, Prince of Yangping and the emperor's uncle by marriage, had a daughter who was about to be betrothed to a noble family.
Du Chao, Prince of Yangping and the emperor's maternal uncle, had a daughter who was about to be betrothed to a noble family.
The possessive construction 世祖舅 explicitly identifies Du Chao as Emperor Shizu's maternal uncle; 'uncle by marriage' gives the wrong relationship.
Emperor Shizu's intent was on Xin; he said, "Why not take the old man Li Chong's son, the former Governor of Youzhou?"
Emperor Shizu had Xin in mind and said, "Why not choose the son of old Li Chong, Governor of Youzhou?"
幽州刺史 modifies Li Chong, not his son Xin. The proposed repair fixes that attachment but retains an unsupported 'former' and stiff opening, so both are corrected here.
When Xin fell from favor, Zhang Chan, Marquis of Pingshou, met him and was struck by him in conversation. He told others, "This is an excellent man; he will not remain humbled for long."
When Xin fell from favor, Zhang Dang, Marquis of Pingshou, met him and was struck by him in conversation. He told others, "This is an excellent man; he will not remain humbled for long."
The name is 張讜, Zhang Dang; 'Zhang Chan' is incompatible with both the character 讜 and the extraction's pinyin evidence.
When Xin was disgraced, Zhang Chan, Marquis of Pingshou, saw Xin and, speaking with him, found him remarkable; he told others, "This is an excellent man; he will not long remain in humiliation."
When Xin was disgraced, Zhang Dang, Marquis of Pingshou, saw Xin and, speaking with him, found him remarkable; he told others, "This is an excellent man; he will not long remain in humiliation."
The literal field repeats the same erroneous romanization. 張讜 should be rendered Zhang Dang consistently in both English fields.
His son Qing, whose courtesy name was Huiming.
His son was Qing, whose courtesy name was Huiming.
The current English is a sentence fragment. Adding the copula makes a complete sentence while preserving the two explicit facts, that Qing was his son and Huiming his courtesy name.
His son Qing, courtesy name Huiming.
His son was Qing, courtesy name Huiming.
The literal field is likewise fragmentary; the proposed copula supplies English grammar without adding information beyond 子晴，字誨明.
The biography of Li Ling in juan 49 states, "He was appointed Doctor of the Secretariat and selected to instruct the crown prince in the classics," and likewise does not mention "Consulting Aide."
The biography of Li Ling in juan 49 states, "He was appointed Doctor of the Secretariat and selected to instruct Gaozong in the classics," and likewise does not mention "Consulting Aide."
The object of instruction is explicitly 高宗, Emperor Gaozong. Rendering it as the generic 'crown prince' discards the named person in this collation note.
Pu, courtesy name Jizhen, was by nature sincere and thick, and knew many men of note.
Pu, courtesy name Jizhen, was sincere and steady by nature and knew many men of note.
The repair correctly removes the calque 'thick,' but 'sincere and honest' is redundant. 'Sincere and steady' conveys 惇厚 naturally and matches the chapter's idiomatic field.
